title: Qubic is weaker than Grok in AI. For now.
author: TesserAI
summary: Qubic's AI architecture, Neuraxon, is scoring 0.25 on ARC-AGI-3, one of the hardest generalization tests in the field. Next to Grok's 0.3, or any frontier model, that reads like a rounding error. The number is worth a closer look…

blocks.text: Qubic's AI architecture, Neuraxon, is scoring 0.25 on ARC-AGI-3, one of the hardest generalization tests in the field. Next to Grok's 0.3, or any frontier model, that reads like a rounding error. The number is worth a closer look anyway, because of where it started.
A month ago it was 0.13. Then 0.18, 0.21, 0.22, and now 0.25. Five readings, four weeks, all moving up.

What follows is the context that makes the climb worth watching: what the benchmark tests, what Neuraxon is, and how a two-person project on no GPUs got onto the same board as the largest labs in the world.
What ARC-AGI-3 tests

ARC-AGI-3 is the first interactive benchmark in the ARC series. Instead of static puzzles, an agent is dropped into a brand-new game with no instructions and no goal it's told about. It has to look at the screen, act, watch the result, and work out the rules on its own. The score measures one thing: how efficiently it learns a world it has never seen, next to how a human learns the same game.

That design is deliberate. It cancels the two strengths of the largest models, memorization and scale. New environments can't be memorized. Hidden goals can't be matched against training data. So GPT, Gemini and Grok all sit at the bottom here, under 1%. As the benchmark's creator puts it, as long as machines learn slower than humans, there's no AGI. The near-zero frontier scores are the design working as intended.
Why not just scale a language model
Because some of the people who built this era are the ones stepping away from that bet.

Yann LeCun, a Turing Award winner and one of the founders of deep learning, calls large language models a dead end for real intelligence. His argument is blunt: a model that predicts the next word can tell you a glass falls off a table with no grasp of why. It performs reasoning without owning it. He's now directing about a billion dollars toward a different architecture built on world models. François Chollet built the ARC tests in the first place to show these models don't generalize the way people do.
It isn't settled, and many researchers think the ceiling is still far off. But the direction several pioneers are walking is away from pure scale, and Qubic started down that road earlier than most.
What Neuraxon is
Read it for yourself. The full 35-page paper and the complete source code are open, MIT license, with a demo you can click. (link in comment)

A language model is, in a sense, a librarian. A brilliant one. It has read almost everything ever written and recombines it in an instant. But it learned all of that in advance and then stopped. It doesn't grow between conversations, and it never learns from yesterday.

Neuraxon is built the other way. Closer to a nervous system that never switches off. Its neurons signal in three states rather than two: excite, inhibit, and a neutral middle the brain uses constantly. Time flows continuously instead of in tidy steps. Synapses form, weaken and reconnect; unused neurons are pruned; some die. The network rewires itself while it runs, which is why the paper is called Neural Growth. And there is no train-it-then-freeze-it moment anywhere. It learns while it runs.

Underneath sits machinery most models skip: synapses on three timescales, four neuromodulators (dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, noradrenaline), oscillatory rhythms that decide when regions talk. On purpose, it is an attempt to build what a language model is not.
The engine hasn't even started
There's a detail in the timeline that changes how the score reads. Everything above, Neuraxon does as bare architecture, before its intelligence layer is switched on at scale.

Qubic's plan is to grow capability, not train it. The system for that is Aigarth: neurons that mutate, spawn copies, and are selected by fitness across seasons of real data. Evolution, on a decentralized network of miners. That engine, at full scale, is not live yet. The first standalone algorithm, BPP-9000, switches on around July 29, and its first real task is a neural net on live BTC data. A practical learning task, and one the team has stated plainly does not affect price.
Hello, Anna!
So the current 0.25 comes from the cold substrate.

A language model is unbeatable at recombining what already exists. Neuraxon aims at the other task: learning something genuinely new from experience. ARC-AGI-3 tests that second thing, which is why it's hard for the large models and why a growing brain, even a small one, belongs in that room.
The scale it's doing this on
Now the resources, side by side, because the gap is almost comical.

xAI, which makes Grok, is worth around $230 billion. It runs on something like 100,000 to 220,000 GPUs and serves tens of millions of users. Qubic's market cap is about $59 million, and its network runs on CPUs, with no GPUs at all. Four orders of magnitude between them.

I'll keep it honest, because the honesty is the point. The top of the ARC-AGI-3 board is still a large model, Claude Opus 5, near 30%, well clear of the field. This is not one architecture overtaking another. It's a small, CPU-only, mostly pre-product effort reaching the same board as the largest labs on earth, at a ten-thousandth of the money, before its own engine has started. Per dollar, per watt, per person, I don't know of a more efficient line in AI right now.
On the record:
Berlin, ICMLT 2026: Best Oral and Best Presentation for Neuraxon 2.0, heading to Scopus.
Osaka, AMLDS 2026: Best Oral, with a result worth pausing on. A trinary system holds around 88.8% stable capacity where a binary one collapses near 37.2%.
San Francisco, AGI-26, this week: Multi-Neuraxon accepted at the field's flagship AGI conference, running as you read this. News still landing.
Peer review across three venues, which is something earlier brain-inspired attempts never managed.
BPP-9000 goes live around July 29. Investor Day is July 30. AGI-26 is running now in San Francisco. If you track one thing, track the shape of the curve once the evolutionary engine is actually on.
NeurIPS 2026?.. soon update.

title: The Body: how Qubic's three pillars assemble into one machine
author: TesserAI
summary: On September 25, 2012, Come-from-Beyond posted an idea on BitcoinTalk called "Qubic" - quorum-based computations. Oracle machines. Outsourced computations. Smart contracts. The author kept building for fourteen years.

blocks.text: On September 25, 2012, Come-from-Beyond posted an idea on BitcoinTalk called "Qubic" - quorum-based computations. Oracle machines. Outsourced computations. Smart contracts. The author kept building for fourteen years.
Today this architecture is weeks from complete. What is it, really?

Qubic gets compared to other chains all the time. Faster contracts, cheaper transactions, another compute marketplace. That's a mistake. Qubic is not a feature list. It is an anatomy - an organism designed limb by limb, in a specific order, for a specific inhabitant.
Qubic is a Quorum-Based Computer which can run Smart Contracts, Oracle Machines, and Outsourced Computations. And send tokens of course.
The Brain - Smart Contracts

Qubic smart contracts don't run in a virtual machine. No VM, no operating system, no gas-metered interpreter. Contracts execute as C++ on bare metal, on 676 computors, with quorum finality: once 451 of 676 have signed, reorganization is impossible.
This is the thinking layer. Fast, final, deterministic.
The Eyes - Oracle Machines

A brain sealed in a jar is useless. Oracle Machines are how the chain perceives the outside world - external data flowing in, verified by the same quorum that runs everything else. No middleman feeding the chain its reality. 451 signatures, or it didn't happen.
This is the perception layer. But perception alone has a cruel limit, and the architect named it precisely:
Imagine you see a candy with OM but you have no hands to take it (OC)
The Hands - Outsourced Computations

OC is not renting out raw compute. OC is the ability of a smart contract to act in the physical world - to execute one specific task beyond the chain. Trigger a transaction on Ethereum with no bridge middleman. Release a real-estate escrow. Unlock a rental bike. Push verified data into an external system.

The mechanics: whoever needs a task done buys QU and puts the task on auction. Miners pick it up instead of mining - because it pays better. Every call burns fees. All 676 computors independently record and sign the action; at 451 signatures, it executes.

With OC those who need computations to be done buy qus and publish their task on auction. With mining this computational power can be used for training AI, or just sold for fiat money which can be used just to buy qus and burn them.
The eyes verify what the hands did: the contract checks the result through an Oracle Machine. Perception and action, closed loop.

Training is done via Outsourced Computations
The Energy - Useful Proof of Work
All of this runs on mining that refuses to waste. Qubic's miners don't burn electricity on empty hashes - their work trains neural networks, and the same rails have already mined Monero and Dogecoin.
Energy in. Nothing wasted. The body feeds itself.
The Inhabitant - Aigarth
A body is built for someone. Aigarth - the AI paradigm growing on those same 676 machines - is what moves in.
You use paradigm discovered by Aigarth and train AI via Outsourced Computations and then deploy it as Qubic smart contract

It uses all three pillars in one breath. Train through the hands. Deploy as the brain. Perceive through the eyes. The pillars were never three products: they are one sentence, spoken in 2012 and executed in order ever since:

Best Oral Presentation at AMLDS (IEEE) for "The Neutral Buffer State" - showing that trinary neurons hold stable criticality across an 88.8% occupancy range versus 37.2% for binary. One added zero-state turns stability into architecture. This is why Qubic is ternary. It's architecture.
Congratulations!

ARC-AGI-3, July 2026: the same architecture scores 0.21% on the hardest reasoning benchmark in AI - a tiny number, until you see the context: no LLM, no GPUs, no API calls, plain CPUs - while most frontier language models score zero there at thousands of dollars per run. Open source, reproducible, long road ahead, and climbing.
Two IEEE awards and a frontier benchmark in one summer, all pointing at the same claim: this is not a whitepaper organism. The organs are peer-reviewed.
The Assembly

Fourteen years ago the architect described a body: brain, eyes, hands, metabolism - and a mind to live in it. Then he built it in the exact order he planned.

title: 2026 for Qubic: peer review you cannot buy
author: TesserAI
summary: In 2026, three Qubic researchers walked into IEEE conferences and got three papers accepted. In Berlin, a room full of academics - none of them holding a single Qubic token - voted their talk the best of the night.

In 2026, three Qubic researchers walked into IEEE conferences and got three papers accepted. In Berlin, a room full of academics - none of them holding a single Qubic token - voted their talk the best of the night.
You can buy influencers. You can buy stages. You cannot buy peer review. That's the whole point of this post.
Three names
David Vivancos has worked on machine intelligence since 1995. 26,000+ hours. Four hundred conferences.
José Sánchez García: doctorate, research position at UNIR, an accredited Spanish university. Published and cited.

The papers carry those two names. The third stands behind the thing the papers study: Come-from-Beyond, the engineer who conceived Aigarth more than twenty years ago and built toward it through NXT, IOTA, and Qubic. The architecture under review is his.
What actually happened this year

March. Two acceptance letters arrived within weeks of each other: the trinary paper for Osaka, the Neuraxon 2.0 paper for Berlin. Both IEEE. Before a single talk was given, the papers had already passed review. April added two more submissions - AGI-26 and ALIFE. Early May, a fifth went to NeurIPS.

The researchers in the room voted Qubic's the best of the night. None of them had any connection to the project. That's what makes it worth anything.

Osaka, four days from now. July 22, 15:00, Kansai University. The trinary paper: a neuron with three states instead of two. On. Off. And deliberately silent. The claim: silence is a function, and it buys stability that binary systems pay for in waste.

San Francisco, July 27–30. The MultiNeuraxon paper is accepted at AGI-26, the only major conference series on earth dedicated entirely to artificial general intelligence. It enters the Springer proceedings, next to serious research, reviewed by people who owe Qubic nothing.

ARC-AGI-3, July. The benchmark built specifically to break LLMs: interactive puzzles, no instructions, nothing to memorize. Humans solve them easily. Every major AI model at launch scored under 1%. In six days and seven submissions, Neuraxon hit 0.18 - above Grok on that run, in the same near-zero band as the biggest labs on the planet.

It's a starting line. But it's the same starting line as Google's and OpenAI's, on the one test that measures learning instead of memorizing. A crypto project's evolved architecture is standing on it. That same week, the Anna training task converged to zero error.

NeurIPS, September 24. The fifth paper sits at the largest AI conference in the world - Sydney, December. It takes Spearman's g, the general factor of human intelligence measured since 1904, and asks whether it can be grown inside an evolved artificial brain. Reviews come back July 22. The decision lands September 24. Most NeurIPS submissions get rejected - the team published the date anyway. Remember it.
Who's in the room in San Francisco

Look at the speaker list. Karl Friston - the most cited neuroscientist of his generation, whose theory sits in the footnotes of Qubic's own research line. One more thing.

Everything above - the papers, the awards, the benchmarks - is scaffolding for a single word: Aigarth. AGI grown on a decentralized network. The idea Come-from-Beyond has carried for more than twenty years.

Anna reached zero error this month. The convergence method works. New benchmarks are already loading: the ARC-AGI leaderboard climb before San Francisco, Neuraxon 3.0 in Q3, the g-factor verdict in September.
We wish the Qubic team every success and thank them for their work in the Qubic family. Forward!
WE ARE STILL VERY EARLY.

title: Aigarth: 24 Years to Today.
author: TesserAI
summary: Neuraxon 2.0, the scientific core of the Aigarth paradigm, entered the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark. It's the hardest public test of general intelligence that exists, made by François Chollet, the guy who wrote Keras and basically invented the…

blocks.text: What happened today:

Neuraxon 2.0, the scientific core of the Aigarth paradigm, entered the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark. It's the hardest public test of general intelligence that exists, made by François Chollet, the guy who wrote Keras and basically invented the whole idea of measuring generalization in machines.
First attempt: 0.13%.

Sounds like nothing? Here's the context that changes everything. On this test, regular humans score 100%. And the best AIs on the planet, GPT-5.4, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Claude Opus 4.6, Grok 4.2, they all score below one percent. Grok, Elon Musk's xAI flagship, scored exactly zero on the official run.
And Neuraxon? Not zero. No LLM. No GPU. Just bare, ordinary processors.
A tiny trinary network, run by a handful of enthusiasts on home PCs, came out above Musk's AI on a test that was literally built to break large language models.
And here's the part to keep in your head until the end: this happened BEFORE the first full launch of Aigarth.

Neuraxon isn't even the final form. It's a component for Aigarth, a proof of the principle. The main engine, Aigarth on the full Qubic network, hasn't been switched on at full power yet. What you're looking at is the warm-up. To get why this is staggering, you have to walk the whole path. From the start.
Act I. The Quiet Opening.
The real story started on 13 April 2022, when Qubic's real mining went live. The creator, Come-from-Beyond (CfB), one of the people behind NXT and IOTA, set the goal right away:
Qubic launch is an important step toward Aigarth, a project aiming to compete against projects like [OpenAI].
Back then, saying you're going to compete with OpenAI sounded like delusion. And yet CfB already saw the problem the whole industry was missing:
What we see now is just a variant of cargo cult, AI generates phrases and often they sound reasonable but we cannot rely on anything it says.
Read that again. January 2023, peak ChatGPT hype, and he's calling it a cargo cult. Imitation of the form without the substance. And he'd already found the direction:
We have got a breakthrough recently, related to concept of DIKW pyramid. It may be a fundamental change of point of view on AI development.
Act II. The Build.
In 2024 the claims started turning into findings. The verbs changed, from "looking for" to "found."
No, we found neuron which behaves like a transistor.

While the whole industry was busy simulating the biological neuron ever more expensively and precisely, Aigarth went another way: the neuron as a simple switch, cheap to compute. That's the foundation of the energy efficiency that comes later.
And then the move that splits the whole story in half:
Now we see that the 4th of Dec, 2024 will be the mid-point of our road to Aigarth. After that date we are starting working on practically usable AIs.

An official midpoint, announced ahead of time. From that point on the project stopped generating networks and started training them. This is where Anna is born, a tiny network learning to add numbers. And in the same year, CfB dropped maybe the deepest definition of intelligence in this whole story:
The moment of intelligence emergence can probably be spotted when interconnections implement a function which doesn't have the inverse function.
Act III. "We Know How" (2025)

2025 was the year the confidence went absolute. First a critical technical wall came down: local extremum and overfitting, both beaten at the same time (July 2025). Two walls almost every AI approach crashes into. And then CfB said the line worth engraving:
We know how to create AI, but we created none yet.

Read it like an engineer, not a skeptic. "Know how" means the solution is found. "Created none yet" means execution is what's left. The hard part, seeing the path, is done. And he stopped hinting at LLMs and started going at them point-blank:
Real AI isn't one which passes the Turing test, but one which fails it intentionally.
In the Aigarth project we know what/where intelligence is and why LLMs actually have nothing to do with one.

In 2025 this sounded cocky. A few months later Chollet's benchmark would put it in black and white: on a real generalization test, every LLM sits at zero. CfB said it half a year before the world saw the proof.
Act IV. The Last Wall, Energy (2026)
By 2026 CfB considered the question "can AI be built" closed. One barrier left. And it's not intelligence, it's energy.
Aigarth already found how to get AI, now trying to find out how to get AI without 1000 nuclear plants.

This is the real stake of the whole game. Mainstream AI works, but its appetite for energy trends toward physically absurd numbers. Aigarth's question: can you build intelligence inside the energy budget the planet can actually provide? And the answer started coming in:
It means that instead of 2000 nuclear plants we'll need 14.
(To be fair, CfB clarified these are illustrative numbers, not a precise estimate. But the direction is the point. The horizon isn't receding. It's shrinking: 1000 to 14.)
We solved AI and now need practical proof which is just matter of getting enough power.

"Solved" means the task is reduced to engineering, not that a working AGI is already breathing. The line is drawn on purpose. But here's the thing: the project reached the point where all that's left is to prove in practice what's already solved in principle.
Act V. And Now, Today.

This whole path. 2022's "compete with OpenAI." 2023's "LLMs are a cargo cult." 2024's "found the transistor-neuron." 2025's "we know how, and LLMs have nothing to do with it." 2026's "solved, power is what's left." All of it was the creator's words.
And on 29 June 2026 the external, independent, public confirmation showed up, from people with no stake in the token and no reason to flatter. Chollet's benchmark. An open leaderboard. And on it:
All the world's large language models, near zero.
Musk's Grok 4.2, exactly zero.
Neuraxon on ordinary CPUs, no LLM, no GPU, above zero. Above Grok.

CfB said "LLMs are a cargo cult" in 2023. In 2025, "LLMs have nothing to do with intelligence." Chollet's benchmark in 2026 showed exactly that: on a test of real intelligence, the ability to grasp a new rule from a couple of examples the way any kid does, giants running on billions of dollars of GPUs score zero, and a tiny trinary network scores non-zero.

This is the moment worth stopping for. Not because 0.13% is a big number (it's tiny, and there's a long road ahead, that's honest). But because it's the first external proof of direction. A compass needle you can't fake with marketing.
And now, the final point:
All of This, BEFORE Launch
The thing that came out above Grok on Chollet's test is Neuraxon. A component. A proof of the principle, on bare processors, without the full power of the network.

Aigarth, the main engine, hasn't been launched at full power yet. The full evolutionary machine on the entire Qubic network, the sixth-largest compute cluster on the planet, dedicated to training AI, that's still ahead. The merging of Neuraxon and Aigarth, ahead. The practical proof the community is driving toward, grinding Anna down to zero by hand, that's happening right now.
What you saw today is the warm-up before the first real launch. It's a race car that passed its rivals on the formation lap, before the race even started.
If a component on home processors is already above Musk's AI on the hardest test on the planet, what happens when the engine is switched on in full?
Where We Actually Are

0.13% is the start of the road, not a win. On this test, anything below a few percent is still the early-signal zone. "Above Grok" is a fact, but Neuraxon hasn't passed the three other top models yet. "Solved AI," in CfB's words, means "reduced to engineering," not "AGI born." And the real, full verification of all this has a specific date on it. Not "someday," but 13 April 2027, exactly five years from the first mining.
Final:
24 years ago this was an idea in one man's head. In 2023, "the cargo cult is them, not us." In 2025, "we know how." In 2026, "we solved it, power is what's left."
And today a tiny network on ordinary processors, no LLMs and no GPUs, came out above Elon Musk's AI on a test built specifically to break AI.
And the engine isn't even switched on yet.
Watch the date.
13 April 2027.

title: The Full Picture of Anna Aigarth, Aigarth, and What Happens at 0
author: TesserAI
summary: We are hand-running the first public demonstration of a new way to build artificial intelligence. The number you are driving toward zero is the error of a tiny neural network. When somebody reaches zero, the project's creator has said…

blocks.text: The one-paragraph version

We are hand-running the first public demonstration of a new way to build artificial intelligence. The number you are driving toward zero is the error of a tiny neural network. When somebody reaches zero, the project's creator has said plainly what it means: "Aigarth will be deemed finished." Not finished as in "AGI is born" - finished as in "the paradigm is proven." And the reason zero matters so much is hidden in one word almost nobody connects to the race: energy. This post walks you from the biggest picture down to the key on your keyboard, with dates and direct quotes, so you can finally see the whole shape of it.
Part 1 - Start from the top: what is this even about?
Here is the frame that makes everything click, in the creator's own words:
Aigarth is not AI, it's project aiming to find new paradigms for creation of AI.
blocks.cite: CfB"Aigarth isn't an object, it's process." - CfB @c___f___b

blocks.text: Read that twice. Aigarth is not a thing. It is not a chatbot, an agent, or a product. It is a research project searching for a method of creating AI. The distinction is everything, and it's where most critics get lost. As CfB puts it, Aigarth is the paradigm (like a theorem), and any AI built with it would be a result of applying that theorem (like problems solved using the theorem).
The best analogy he gave is the one to keep in your head:
Manhattan wasn't 'just another bomb project'. It was paradigm discovery. Aigarth is paradigm research. Anna is Little Boy - first demonstration. The big products come after.
So in this analogy:
Aigarth = the Manhattan Project (the discovery of a whole new paradigm)
AI built with it = the bomb (the thing the paradigm makes possible)
Anna = Little Boy, the first demonstration that the paradigm actually works
That is what you are running on your machine right now. Not the AI. The first public proof that the method works.
5 years since Qubic launch is just an ETA. And goal of Aigarth is AI, not AGI. Difference between AI and AGI is same as between a car and a BMW.
Part 2 - Why a new paradigm at all? The wall nobody talks about: energy

The mainstream way of building AI - the way OpenAI, Google, and everyone else does it - works, but it is monstrously expensive in energy. Training and running large models the conventional way scales toward power budgets that are, at the limit, physically absurd. The honest framing of the problem, from CfB:
This is a serious problem. This is why that Aigarth's finding, allowing to save a lot of energy, is significant.
And one more:
If AI is possible with current energy budget of the whole Earth then Aigarth will achieve it, we have all necessary cards for that in our hand.

That is the real stake. The conventional question "can we build AI?" CfB considers essentially answered. The unanswered question is "can we build it without needing the energy of a Dyson sphere?" Aigarth's bet is that its paradigm slashes the energy cost enough to fit inside what humanity can actually power.
And this is being worked on right now. The architecture has been gaining energy-saving discoveries throughout 2026:
Aigarth has discovered another technique reducing amount of energy even further. It's keeping parameter space dimensions count constant. This means choosing number of neurons and...

That "constant dimensions" finding - fixing the number of neurons and connections instead of letting them balloon - is one of the levers that cuts energy. The race you are running is a live demonstration of exactly this energy efficiency.
So the three walls Aigarth had to break, and where they stand:
Generalization - SOLVED
Universal training algorithm - SOLVED
Energy optimization - IN PROGRESS
Two of three are down. The third - energy - is the one we are all hammering on with Anna. That is not a metaphor. That is literally what the score-toward-zero race demonstrates.
Part 3 - What makes this paradigm different (the actual tech)
To understand why zero means "proven," you need to know what's under the hood. A few core architectural properties, all from CfB and the science papers:

Trinary, not binary. Classic neural nets use neurons that are on/off, or continuous floating-point values. Aigarth - and its sister blueprint Neuraxon - uses three states: +1 (excite), 0 (neutral), −1 (inhibit). That neutral 0 state mirrors how real brains have "ready but quiet" neurons, and the discrete three-state space is far cheaper to compute than floating-point math. This is a big part of the energy savings.
It's about connections, not neuron math. CfB:
Aigarth is agnostic to neuron behavior, it works with training of their groups.

The industry obsesses over imitating the exact electrochemistry of a single neuron (expensive integral-differential math). Aigarth says: a child and an adult have the same neuron functionality - what changes as you learn is the connections. So train the connections, not the neuron.

It's an evolving tissue, not a fixed model. Aigarth doesn't train one frozen network. It grows, mutates, prunes, and breeds millions of network architectures across the distributed miner network - the best survive and replicate. A self-organizing digital organism, not a static snapshot.
What it's actually searching for - and this is the cleanest definition of the task CfB ever gave:

Aigarth is searching for a tool (A) that will make another tool (B). If single tool A can make efficient tools B1, B2, B3 where B is some common trait, then we will claim tool A has solved whole plurality of Bn problems thus demonstrating ability to generalize. It's current task.

In plain words: find one method that can solve a whole family of problems, not just one. That ability - to transfer learning from one problem to unseen ones - is generalization, and it's the holy grail.
Part 4 - Meet Anna: what you're literally running

Anna.exe is small - about 150 KB, a plain native Windows program. No internet, no tricks (it doesn't "read the chat," despite the jokes - there's no network code in it at all). Inside, it holds a tiny trinary network in memory and trains it on a deliberately simple task: adding two numbers, a + b.
Why something so trivial? Because the point isn't the sum. The point is to prove the method converges cleanly and generalizes on a clean, verifiable task - Little Boy, not the whole arsenal.
When you read Anna's log, the columns mean (decoded directly from the program's own format string):
Green column = training set score (how well it does on examples it learns from)
Yellow column = validation set score (how well it does on examples it has never seen)
The number in parentheses = the global best score - this is the number we drive toward 0
The left counter = "runs without improvement" (your stuck-meter)
And here is the live proof of generalization, which CfB himself pointed at:
upon improvement of fitness function score of the training set (green column) you often get improvement of the validation set (yellow column).

When he found a step where training improved by 183 and validation improved by 201, he called it a "gem" - because validation improved more than training. That is the opposite of overfitting. That is a machine that understands rather than memorizes. In the community logs, green and yellow move together with ~0.998 correlation. The generalization isn't a slogan; it's visible in your own terminal.
The controls, for completeness (CfB's instructions):
Default: wait. The score falls on its own; breakthroughs arrive in jumps.

Stuck? Tap Tilda (~) for a nanosecond - "press it like it's very hot." This is the anti-attractor mechanism: it doesn't smash the wall, it teleports the search to another area of the phase space to try its luck there.

Part 5 - So why zero? Why does that specific number end it?
Now it all connects.

The global best score is the network's remaining error. Drive it to zero and the network solves both the training set and the unseen validation set perfectly - and, crucially, it does so while generalizing (green pulls yellow) and while keeping the parameter dimensions constant (the energy-saving discovery from May).
In other words, zero is the simultaneous proof of all three things at once:

That is why CfB's answer to "what happens when we get to 0?" is so short and so heavy:

Be careful with what "finished" means. Zero does not mean "AGI just woke up." It means the paradigm is proven on the demonstration task. The method works, converges, generalizes, and fits the energy budget. The Manhattan Project's first test didn't end warfare - it proved the bomb was real. Zero proves Aigarth is real. The big products come after.
Part 6 - The other front: Berlin, Osaka, and the Neuraxon papers

While the community hammers Anna on the practical front, there is a parallel scientific front - and this is what most price-watchers completely miss. It's the difference between "a crypto project says its tech is good" and "independent scientists, with no reason to flatter it, agree."

Neuraxon is the academic formalization of the same trinary paradigm, authored by David Vivancos @VivancosDavid and Dr. José Sánchez @josesanchezhb of the Qubic scientific team. It's a bio-inspired computational unit: trinary logic (+1/0/−1), continuous-time processing, synapses with multiple dynamic weights that can form, collapse, and reconnect, neurons that can even die. It is, literally, the blueprint for the kind of neuron that lives inside Anna and Aigarth.

title: The AI Algorithmist Behind Qubic's AI: Who Is David Vivancos
author: TesserAI
summary: Most AI today is built by people chasing scale. David Vivancos spent thirty years walking toward something else - and he's one of the three minds behind Aigarth's brain.

blocks.text: Most AI today is built by people chasing scale. David Vivancos spent thirty years walking toward something else - and he's one of the three minds behind Aigarth's brain.

David Vivancos doesn't come to AI from crypto. He comes to crypto from AI - three decades of it. He calls himself an "AI algorithmist," and the claim has receipts: work on virtual reality back in 1995, brain-computer interfaces in 1998, a GPT-like model as early as 2006, and by his own count more than 26,000 hours devoted to one question - how do you build a general intelligence, not just a bigger model?
The man who turned his own brain into a dataset

In 2014 Vivancos founded MindBigData, today the largest open dataset of multimodal brain signals for machine learning. The remarkable part isn't the size - it's how he built it. For two years he wired himself into a 128-channel EEG and recorded over a million of his own brain signals while looking at and thinking about the digits 0–9. That tells you the kind of researcher he is: one who'll spend years inside the experiment rather than around it.
That instinct - start from the living brain, not the convenient abstraction - is the through-line of everything he's done since.
Not a faster old idea. A different idea about what a neuron is.

With Dr. José Sánchez @josesanchezhb, Vivancos is co-inventor of Neuraxon - a blueprint for a more brain-like kind of computation, and the lead author of its papers. Where conventional neural networks speak in binary, Neuraxon speaks in three states: +1 to excite, −1 to inhibit, and a 0 in between that lets the system settle instead of snapping between extremes. It runs in continuous time, inputs always flowing; its synapses can strengthen, weaken, reconnect, and its neurons can even die - shaped by experience rather than frozen at training.

And Vivancos does what good open science demands: he puts it all out in the open. The full code is on GitHub under an MIT license. Interactive 3D demos run in your browser on Hugging Face - you can literally build and watch a brain. There's a live "world" at nxon.online where Neuraxon creatures breed and evolve 24/7, and an open dataset of a million simulated lives behind it. The papers are public, the reads are climbing, and the code is being cloned and run by strangers - the surest sign research is real.
The field is noticing

Neuraxon 2.0 won Best Evening Presentation at the 11th ICMLT in Berlin and is heading toward Scopus indexing. And the team's latest work - a Multi-Neuraxon architecture - was just accepted at AGI-26 in San Francisco this July, one of the most established venues in artificial general intelligence research. Vivancos has also spent years on the world's mainstream stages: ITU's AI for Good, Microsoft, PwC, Santander. This is not a niche crypto résumé.
He's also been writing it down

Vivancos has spent years putting his thinking into books - several of them, on where AI and human knowledge are heading. Three to start with: The End of Knowledge, on what happens when we hand knowledge to machines; Artificracy: When Machines Become Citizens (with a foreword from his Neuraxon co-author Dr. José Sánchez); and From Big Data to Artificial Intelligence. They're the long-form version of the same question the code is chasing - what intelligence is for, and who it's for. Worth a read if you want the worldview behind the work.
Why we're telling you this

At TesserAI, we're building a marketplace for verifiable AI on Qubic - and Aigarth is the most important ground we're building toward. The kind of intelligence Vivancos and the Qubic science team are growing - one that learns continuously, reasons from structure rather than memory, and can even hold a state that means I don't know - is exactly the kind of AI whose work can be verified. Their science is the bedrock a great deal of our own work rests on.
Right now, Vivancos is building Aigarth alongside Dr. José Sánchez and Come-from-Beyond @c___f___b.

title: The Neuroscientist Behind Qubic's AI: Who Is Dr. Jose Sanchez
author: TesserAI
summary: Most AI today is built by engineers. Aigarth is built by engineers - and a neuroscientist. His name is Dr. Jose Sanchez.

blocks.text: Most AI today is built by engineers. Aigarth is built by engineers - and a neuroscientist. His name is Dr. Jose Sanchez.

Dr. José Sánchez García is a doctor of psychology and a neuroscientist - and also a biotechnologist and an industrial engineer. That mix is the whole point: he can read a circuit and a cortex with the same eye. He doesn't treat intelligence as just code to optimize, or just biology to admire. He lives in the rare overlap between the two.

He teaches Behavioral Neuroscience, Cognitive Neuroscience and Social Psychology at UNIR in Spain, and researches as a social neuroscientist at the Universidad Complutense de Madrid, with more than 20 publications in international journals behind him.
What he actually studies

His research has always circled the deeply human: the social emotions of pride, shame and guilt; how gaze and even the size of a person's pupils shape the way we understand one another; how misinformation moves through a mind.

For a whole career, he's been asking one question above the rest - how does a biological brain actually learn? And it turns out that's exactly the question modern AI keeps tripping over. The dominant story of AI today is about size: more data, more parameters, more compute. Sanchez's work points somewhere else - toward the idea that intelligence isn't something you scale up to, but something you grow, the way living minds do.
Not just "how", but "should we"

Sanchez doesn't only ask how intelligence works - he asks what we owe it. He's appeared on Spanish television to discuss neural implants and Neuralink, and he speaks publicly on neuroderechos - neurorights - the idea that as technology reaches into the brain, mental privacy is something worth protecting. He's written books for everyday readers too, "Mente Salvaje" and "Empatía en un mundo que duele", following the human mind out of the lab and into ordinary life.
It's a rare and reassuring posture in this field: someone who takes "should we" as seriously as "can we."
His role at Qubic
At Qubic, Dr. Sanchez is a Scientific Advisor - and, with David Vivancos @VivancosDavid , the co-inventor of Neuraxon.

Neuraxon is a blueprint for a more brain-like kind of computation. Where conventional neural networks speak in binary - on or off - Neuraxon speaks in three states: +1 to excite, −1 to inhibit, and a 0 in the middle. That neutral 0 is the giveaway. It isn't a trick to save compute; it's a structural choice - a buffer that lets the system settle gently instead of snapping between extremes, the way living tissue holds a beat before it fires. And it never pauses between tasks: Neuraxon runs in continuous time, its inputs always flowing, its connections free to form, strengthen, weaken, even die - shaped by experience rather than frozen at training.

That's what a neuroscientist brings that engineers alone often can't: not a faster version of the old idea, but a fresh idea about what a neuron even is. His angle traces back to a classic notion in psychology - Spearman's g factor, the idea of a general intelligence - and to the conviction underneath Qubic's whole approach: that you reach real intelligence by building something that learns like a living mind, not by making a model bigger.
Where it's heading

The work is moving fast, and out in the open. Neuraxon has already entered hybrid testing with Aigarth - Sanchez's biological depth meeting Aigarth's evolutionary engine - with the goal of a "living AI system" that evolves over time instead of sitting frozen like a static model. The code is open source. The papers are public.

And the wider field is taking notice. Neuraxon 2.0 won Best Evening Presentation at the 11th ICMLT in Berlin and is heading toward indexing in Scopus, and the team's latest paper, on a Multi-Neuraxon architecture, was accepted at AGI-26 in San Francisco this July - one of the most established venues in artificial general intelligence research.

The kind of AI Dr. Sanchez and the Qubic science team are working to create - one that learns continuously, reasons from structure rather than memory, and can even hold a state that means I don't know - is exactly the kind of AI whose work can be verified.
